Never assume a replica is current; it is eventually consistent.
Replay is single-threaded: one startup process.
A parallel write workload outruns any replica disk.
Replay wants to remove a row version a query still needs.
Five types: snapshot, lock, tablespace, buffer pin, deadlock.

blocks.title: The feedback tax
blocks.text: One forgotten idle-in-transaction session on a replica blocks `VACUUM` cluster-wide and bloats the primary.

items: Simplest: `synchronous_commit = remote_apply` for that txn.
Or capture `pg_current_wal_insert_lsn()` right after the write.
Then poll `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()` until it passes.

items: `pg_is_in_recovery()` is the cheap health-check probe.
libpq `target_session_attrs=read-write` finds the writable node.
Replicas cannot create temp tables or write work tables.
Some ORMs and BI tools fail on a standby for that alone.

blocks.q: A report needs a stable snapshot for 40 minutes?
a_bullets: Pause replay on the replica, run it, then resume.
Lag grows while paused: watch disk and slot size.
Or point it at a `recovery_min_apply_delay` replica instead.

blocks.title: Backups off the replica
items: Offloads backup I/O from the primary.
Needs a slot or archive access during the backup.
Otherwise needed WAL is recycled underneath you.
`pg_ctl promote` or `SELECT pg_promote()` ends recovery.
The timeline bumps and the standby becomes writable.
`promote_trigger_file` is deprecated in PG16.
Cascading standbys follow the timeline change automatically.
RPO: data you can lose. Async seconds, sync zero.
RTO: downtime = detection + promotion + client re-routing.
Most teams size RPO and forget the re-routing half of RTO.
